report:
**Conclusion:** The claim appears **true**, not false: randomized-trial evidence shows exemestane lowers *breast-cancer incidence* in postmenopausal women selected for elevated risk.

The pivotal double-blind MAP.3 trial randomized 4,560 such women to exemestane or placebo. At a median 35 months, invasive breast cancer occurred at annual rates of 0.19% versus 0.55%—a hazard ratio of 0.35 (about a **65% relative reduction**). The primary report concludes that exemestane significantly reduced invasive breast cancers in this population.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507

This is not merely an observational association: it was a placebo-controlled randomized trial. NCI’s summary likewise reports a substantial reduction in invasive breast cancer among high-risk postmenopausal participants.  
https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk

**Why skepticism is still reasonable:** the follow-up was short (median about three years), the absolute event rate was low, and the trial was designed to measure cancer incidence—not breast-cancer mortality. Thus, it supports reduced diagnoses (especially hormone-receptor–positive cancers), but does not by itself establish a survival benefit. A review highlights the short follow-up and the need to weigh toxicities, particularly bone and musculoskeletal effects.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/

The clinical implication is selective use: preventive endocrine medicines are considered for women at increased breast-cancer risk who have a low risk of medication harms, rather than for average-risk women.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/evidence-summary/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction
